extracted.intended_audience: corporate legal/compliance teams, in-house counsel, investor_relations and communications professionals at public companies, and PR firms
extracted.subtask_short: Reg FD compliance for public companies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public companies and their communications/PR advisors on complying with SEC Regulation Fair Disclosure (Reg FD), avoiding selective disclosure of material, nonpublic information, and responding to inadvertent disclosures (including via social media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation FD prohibition on selective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation Fair Disclosure (Reg FD) prohibits public companies or persons acting on their behalf from selectively disclosing material, nonpublic information to certain persons outside the company, including holders of company securities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever an issuer or person acting on its behalf discloses material, nonpublic information to company security holders or other specified persons, the regulation requires the company to also disclose the information to the public. Selective disclosures (even unintentional) can trigger Reg FD obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt public disclosure requirement for non-intentional selective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-intentional selective disclosure, Reg FD requires the public disclosure be made 'promptly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation defines 'promptly' as 'as soon as reasonably practicable (but in no event after the later of 24 hours or the commencement of the next day’s trading on the New York Stock Exchange) after a senior official of the issuer . . . learns that there has been a non-intentional disclosure by the issuer or person acting on behalf of the issuer of information that the senior official knows, or is reckless in not knowing, is both material and nonpublic.' Failure to make this prompt public disclosure can result in an enforcement finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality and identification of disclosed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications must be evaluated for whether the information disclosed is material and nonpublic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies must be able to identify when a communication contains material information. Confirmatory later statements (e.g., earnings releases/calls) may demonstrate materiality. Failing to recognize materiality and comply with prompt-disclosure obligations is a key risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and refresh Reg FD disclosure policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a Reg FD disclosure policy in place is necessary but not sufficient; companies should regularly circulate and refresh policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make policies accessible, provide regular Reg FD training to insiders (including directors) and employees with corporate communications responsibilities, and review policies periodically to reflect changes in technology, communications trends, and SEC guidance. (Example: SEC settlement required DraftKings to provide training within 30 days.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and authorize who may speak for the company
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit who is authorized to communicate on the company’s behalf about financial/operational matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should restrict authorized spokespersons, especially during quiet periods, and ensure communications are part of the company’s disclosure controls and procedures. Closely monitor communications from authorized individuals and take prompt action to address inadvertent disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party PR firms must comply with company disclosure policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies are responsible for communications made by third-party PR firms acting on their behalf and should ensure such firms comply with Reg FD policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure PR firms are familiar with and agree to follow disclosure policies, closely monitor their outputs for material, nonpublic information, and clarify any circumstances under which they may use personal social media accounts belonging to company insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media-specific requirements for Reg FD compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC recognizes social media can be used to comply with Reg FD if the company has made investors, the market, and the media aware of the channels of distribution it expects to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies wishing to use social media for Reg FD compliance must publicize the channels so stakeholders know where to look. Because social media remains a gray area, most companies should use customary methods (Forms 8-K or press releases) alongside or instead of social media. If relying solely on social media, consult counsel to minimize risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal social media policies and prior approval controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate social media policies should prohibit sharing confidential or financial/performance information on social media except with prior written approval from the communications team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies may explicitly prohibit use of employee/corporate blogs, chat boards, Facebook, Twitter, and similar platforms to disclose material, nonpublic information and should specify restrictions during quiet periods and who qualifies as an authorized spokesperson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing a post does not eliminate Reg FD risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking down a social-media post after it is published does not negate that a selective disclosure occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if communications staff quickly remove a post, selective disclosure to followers may have occurred; the company must still evaluate materiality and, if required, make the required prompt public disclosure. Late official announcements that confirm the content do not cure a failure to promptly disclose under Reg FD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement risk and consequences for Reg FD violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to refresh and diligently comply with Reg FD policies can lead to SEC enforcement actions and penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences can include civil penalties (e.g., DraftKings agreed to pay $200,000), settlement terms requiring training or remediation, and reputational risk. Proactive compliance reduces these risks.
